changes.before:
Disability-led leadership means people with disabilities lead the decisions that shape their own lives and services. The idea grows from self-advocacy, the work of people with disabilities speaking and organizing for themselves and each other, and from families who organized alongside them. Minnesota has a long connection to this work. Partners in Policymaking was created in Minnesota in 1987 as a leadership program for adults with disabilities and parents of young children with developmental disabilities, and the Minnesota Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities offers it today. Its graduates work in partnership with elected officials to improve how people with disabilities live, work and are educated.

Self-determination puts personal choice at the center. The Council's Partners in Living course pairs self-determination with personal choice, person-centered planning and planning for the future, and it notes that a meaningful life does not look the same for everyone. For a leader, the point is practical. A person who lives with a disability and has learned to navigate services holds expertise that professional training does not supply. Disability may be visible or not, and many colleagues bring this expertise to their work as well. Treat it as leadership, not as an inspiring story shared at the start of a meeting and then set aside.

Leading and being consulted are different roles. When people are consulted, staff set the question, write the draft and decide what to do with the comments. When people lead, they help decide what the problem is, what the work should produce and how success will be judged. Many agency processes default to consultation because it is familiar and fits our timelines. Ask yourself where you learned that default and who it leaves out. Then look at one decision in front of you and ask: who is leading here, and whose expertise about disabled lives shapes this decision?

Sharing leadership does not mean handing over decisions that belong to someone else. Laws, funding rules and formal determinations stay with the responsible program area, and legal questions go to legal counsel. What a leader can change is everything around those fixed points: who sets the agenda, who drafts, who presents and who judges whether the result worked. Say plainly which parts are open and which are fixed, so nobody is invited to lead a decision that has already been made. The Council's free online Partners courses are a good way to keep learning from this tradition.

changes.before:
Disability history is a practical tool for leaders today. The Council's Partners in Time course follows how people with developmental disabilities lived, learned and worked from ancient times to today. It describes a long record of discrimination, segregation, abuse, ignorance and silence, including times when kind intentions still produced harmful results. It also traces the changes that moved society toward greater inclusion, and it asks learners to notice how history repeats itself.

Good intentions are not the same as good results. The point about kind intentions matters most for leaders, because harm can come from people who mean well. The pattern to watch for is a decision made about people, without them, for reasons that sound caring: safety, efficiency, specialized help or protection. Those reasons can be real. The risk is that they carry the decision without anyone checking, with the people affected, whether it serves them. A plan that separates people by disability deserves a second look, even when the separation is offered as a kindness.

Four history questions help you test a proposal before it is approved. First, does this plan separate people by disability, and who asked for that? Second, who designed it, and did people who would use it take part from the start? Third, what does the plan assume people cannot do, and what evidence supports that assumption? Fourth, if the people affected disagree, can they change it, decline it or choose something else? Write down the answers before the proposal goes forward, and share them with the people who will decide. When an answer is unclear, treat it as a reason to ask, not as a reason to stop.

Learning from history is not about blaming the people who came before you or the colleagues around you today. Most people in human services chose the work in order to help. The lesson is about systems: habits of deciding for people become routine when nobody asks these questions. When you notice the pattern, name it as a pattern in the process, bring in the people affected, and take questions about eligibility, rights or service decisions to the responsible program area. Partners in Time is free and self-paced, and it is worth taking before your next redesign.

changes.before:
Sharing power starts with a role that carries real decisions. The National Frontline Supervisor Competencies, from the University of Minnesota's Institute on Community Integration, include seeking the views of people receiving supports and their families when organizations develop policies and procedures, and even state and federal rules. The Council's Partners in Making Your Case course teaches self-advocates and families how policy is made, how to meet with policymakers, give testimony and organize with others. The self-advocacy tradition prepares people to act on policy, not only to comment on it.

Habits for involving people can be read along the intercultural development continuum. A Minimization habit treats everyone the same: one meeting format, one comment period, one set of documents, open to all. It feels fair, and it quietly assumes the professional way of meeting is the normal way. An Acceptance habit notices the difference: long midday meetings, dense documents and unpaid time suit staff, whose job this is, and not people who volunteer, work elsewhere or use supports. An Adaptation habit changes the process itself, with members, and then checks with them whether the change worked.

Three practical changes make it possible for people to lead: pay, preparation and shared leadership. First, pay people for their time and expertise, as you would any consultant, and arrange payment before the work starts. Second, prepare and support people: share plain-language materials well ahead, offer a briefing before each meeting, and ask what helps each person take part, whether that is a support person, captions, breaks, another format or time to respond in writing. Disability may be visible or not, so ask everyone rather than guessing. Third, share leadership through a self-advocate co-chair, members setting part of the agenda, and members reviewing what their advice changed.

Paying people and meeting access needs often depend on partners in other areas. Whether and how your area can pay people, through a contract, a stipend or another route, is a question for the responsible program area and its finance and contract staff, with legal counsel where needed. Access requests from public participants go through your area's access process, and employee accommodation questions go to Human Resources. A leader's part is to raise these questions early, budget for them and keep members informed. Be honest about limits: if something cannot be paid or changed, say so and say what you will do instead.

The following meeting patterns are a reflection exercise using terms from the intercultural development continuum. They cannot establish a person’s developmental orientation or substitute for a qualified assessment. A Minimization habit treats everyone the same: one meeting format, one comment period, one set of documents, open to all. It feels fair, and it quietly assumes the professional way of meeting is the normal way. An Acceptance habit notices the difference: long midday meetings, dense documents and unpaid time suit staff, whose job this is, and not people who volunteer, work elsewhere or use supports. An Adaptation habit changes the process itself, with members, and then checks with them whether the change worked.

Three practical supports can make leadership more accessible: compensation, preparation and meaningful decision roles. Seek an authorized way to compensate time and expertise, and confirm funding, eligibility, terms and approval before promising payment or asking people to begin paid work. Second, prepare and support people: share plain-language materials well ahead, offer a briefing before each meeting, and ask what helps each person take part, whether that is a support person, captions, breaks, another format or time to respond in writing. Disability may be visible or not, so ask everyone rather than guessing. Third, share leadership through a self-advocate co-chair, members setting part of the agenda, and members reviewing what their advice changed.

Paying people and meeting access needs often depend on partners in other areas. Whether and how your area can pay people, through a contract, a stipend or another route, is a question for the responsible program area and its finance and contract staff, with legal counsel where needed. Access requests from public participants go through your area's access process, and employee accommodation questions go to Human Resources. A leader's part is to raise these questions early, budget for them and keep members informed. Explain limits early and invite people to choose whether and how to participate. Do not treat willingness to volunteer as evidence that payment barriers are unimportant. Access obligations still apply even when a compensation request cannot be approved.

changes.after: Meaningful participation includes influence over the agenda, preparation, access support and a clear account of what advice changed. Seek approved compensation and explain its terms before participation.

changes.before:
Disability-led leadership has to reach the people who provide support every day. Direct support professionals help people with disabilities live the lives they choose, and their supervisors shape how that support happens. The National Frontline Supervisor Competencies, developed at the University of Minnesota's Research and Training Center on Community Living, describe 11 areas of skill for supervisors of direct support professionals in intellectual and developmental disability services. Three areas speak directly to this course: advocacy and public relations; leadership, professionalism and self-development; and cultural awareness and responsiveness.

The National Frontline Supervisor Competencies treat choice and self-advocacy as part of the supervisor's job. They describe person-centered support that gives people as much choice and control as possible, promoting self-advocacy when someone meets barriers, and teaching advocacy skills to people receiving services, families and staff. They recognize individuals and families as the ultimate decision makers about the services and supports in their lives. They also ask supervisors to seek direct support professionals' ideas, let them make decisions and run meetings that build trust and shared ownership. Keep the limits in mind: the set dates from 2013, was written for provider organizations in intellectual and developmental disability services, and builds on a 2007 study in which direct support staff, supervisors and managers rated how important each skill was, plus expert review. It shows which skills the field values, not that training on them improves outcomes.

You can bring disability-led values into any frontline work you lead or shape. First, ask before you decide: when a change affects how support is given, ask frontline staff and people receiving services what they see, and let their answers change the plan. Second, share decisions with the team, not only tasks, so the people closest to the work help set how it is done. Third, make self-advocacy part of ordinary practice by checking that people know how to raise a concern and who will listen. In state work, the same moves apply when you design training expectations, review provider practice or plan a workforce effort.

Your role has limits when the work belongs to a provider or another area. Supervisors at provider organizations work within their employer's policies, licensing requirements and any labor agreement, and state staff do not direct a provider's personnel decisions. Hiring, discipline and pay questions for agency staff belong with Human Resources and labor relations. Use the competency set as a source of ideas, not as a checklist for rating anyone. The Institute on Community Integration offers it as a free download, and it can open a useful conversation with providers and self-advocates about good frontline leadership.
